reinstatement.title: Reinstatements and Probationary Licenses
reinstatement.intro: These decisions are not new discipline. They granted a petition to reinstate a surrendered or revoked license, or issued a probationary license to an applicant, and are included because they describe the conduct that led to the original action and the conditions imposed on return to practice. Each lists the offense category of that underlying conduct.

appendix.title: Appendix: Physicians Listed with Psychiatry as a Secondary Specialty
appendix.intro: The physicians in these cases list psychiatry among their specialties in public provider registries, but none was found in the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology's certification records, and the decision itself (and in most cases the registries' primary specialty) points to another field: family, internal, addiction or laboratory medicine. They are kept here because the conduct is still instructive.

about: These summaries describe disciplinary actions taken by the Medical Board of California against physicians identified as psychiatrists, drawn from the Board's decision documents linked in its newsletter (Volumes 158-173, roughly 2021-2026). Each entry summarizes what happened leading up to the discipline, usually from the factual allegations in the Accusation or Petition to Revoke Probation attached to the decision, followed by the Board's order.

Most cases were resolved by stipulated settlement, in which the physician typically does not admit the allegations. Entries say "the Accusation alleged" in those cases, and reserve "found" for cases where an administrative law judge or the Board made findings and "admitted" for admissions. Allegations are not proven facts.

Physicians are not named; case IDs (CA-<newsletter volume>-<entry>) map back to the public record through a separate key. Patients are referred to as in the original documents. The decisions are scanned images and were read via OCR, so occasional details may be imperfect; consult the original decision before relying on a specific fact. Each case appears once, under the category of the conduct that most drove it, with any other categories listed beneath its heading.

narrative: This decision granted a petition for reinstatement of a surrendered license; it is included because the reinstatement terms flow from earlier discipline. The psychiatrist had practiced in an academic health system, as program director at a psychiatric hospital, as medical director of an addiction treatment provider, and in private practice. In 2016 the Board filed a First Amended Accusation charging him with sexual abuse, misconduct, and relations with a patient; repeated negligent acts, including prescribing benzodiazepines to that patient, who abused alcohol; general unprofessional conduct; and gross negligence and over-prescribing involving four additional patients. He resolved that Accusation by a stipulated surrender of his license, effective November 2017. The present decision does not describe the details of the underlying conduct further.

At the 2021 reinstatement hearing before an administrative law judge, the psychiatrist admitted the sexual encounter with a patient, acknowledged it was egregious, and expressed remorse. The judge found that he had attended a 12-step program for sex and love addiction since 2012 (serving as a sponsor), had individual psychotherapy until 2018 and ongoing group therapy, had completed a professional boundaries and ethics course in 2013, had worked as a medical content writer since the surrender, had completed substantial CME, and presented supportive testimony and letters. The judge found significant rehabilitation and that reinstatement on probation would not be against the public interest; the Attorney General did not oppose reinstatement.
cases.outcome: Petition for reinstatement granted; license reinstated, revoked, revocation stayed, 3 years' probation with clinical competence assessment program (no practice until completed), total controlled-substance restriction (including no marijuana recommendations), professionalism/ethics program, psychiatric evaluation, psychotherapy, practice monitor, solo practice prohibition, third-party chaperone for female patients, and prohibition on supervising PAs/APNs.

narrative: According to the Accusation, beginning in March 2018 the psychiatrist treated Patient 1, a 29-year-old woman with panic attacks, chronic anxiety, a history of sexual abuse by a partner, and a prior ADHD diagnosis, in an outpatient practice with weekly in-person therapy he described as cognitive behavioral therapy. He allegedly did not obtain prior records, validate the ADHD diagnosis, or document an adequate history; prescribed diazepam routinely and continued as-needed methylphenidate without documented informed consent, rationale, effectiveness review, or CURES check; later added quetiapine for insomnia without documented reasoning; and kept notes that made it hard to tell what therapy was delivered. He also reviewed the patient's social media, including photographs, and discussed it in sessions. By mid-2018 he charted her transference attraction and his own countertransference, a curbside consult, and a referral to a therapist that she declined, but he continued treating her. Text messages, his interview with Board investigators, and her complaint allegedly showed escalating boundary violations: calling himself a 'pick-up artist,' saying they would 'probably be hooking up' if both were single, continuing therapy after learning she was the person he had been chatting with in a sexually provocative way in an online game chat room, asking her during a video session to show her breasts, and making a sexually explicit remark.

In a January 2019 in-person session, by the patient's account, he unzipped her dress, breathed along her back, neck, and inner thighs, touched her, and kissed her forehead; he told investigators he traced her exposed skin with his lips and face. He charted a 'clear significant boundary violation' without details, yet kept contacting her by text, video, and in person after purportedly referring her elsewhere, calling her his 'favorite patient.' The Accusation charged sexual misconduct, gross negligence, unprofessional conduct, and inadequate records. He did not admit the allegations but agreed a prima facie case or factual basis could be established.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 7 years' probation with 40 hours/year education, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, and professional boundaries program (the latter three already satisfied), psychiatric evaluation, psychotherapy, practice monitor, prohibition on accepting new female patients (with patient notification log), probation disclosure to patients under B&P 2228.1, prohibition on supervising PAs/APNs, and probation monitoring costs.

narrative: Patient A, an adult woman with OCD, panic disorder, and ADHD who reported recent thoughts that suicide might be the only way to stop her panic, began outpatient treatment with the psychiatrist in October 2019 while another physician was prescribing her alprazolam, Adderall, and carisoprodol. According to the Accusation, the psychiatrist replaced alprazolam with lorazepam and took over and increased Adderall without contacting the other prescriber, never obtained or documented releases to coordinate with her other providers, did not document informed consent for controlled substances, and gave a "courtesy fill" of a progestin-only contraceptive based on the patient's report of her gynecologist's advice without reviewing the gynecologist's labs. In spring 2020 the patient told him she was sexually attracted to him, which he did not document. In June 2020 emails, when she asked whether she should transfer care because she wanted a sexual relationship with him, he acknowledged a "connection/tension" and encouraged her to continue treatment; when she asked him to write a sexual fantasy about her, he replied that he was happy to do so. None of these emails were in the chart.

The Accusation further alleged that on July 3, 2020, without prior notice, he discharged her (citing a clinic closing) with a three-month supply of medications and told her they could be friends; a sexual relationship began within days by her account (late July by his, as he acknowledged to Board investigators) and continued through the summer. In September 2020 he wrote her further prescriptions for Adderall, fluoxetine, and lorazepam. Her subsequent therapist documented treatment for the effects of the relationship and worsening of her conditions. Charges included sexual misconduct, sexual exploitation, gross negligence (including improper termination), repeated negligent acts, inadequate records, and unprofessional conduct. The psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established and surrendered his license; no findings were made.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; not eligible for reinstatement under the statutory bar for surrender based on sexual misconduct/exploitation; cost recovery of $94,244.00 payable before any new or reinstated license.

narrative: Patient A, a 45-year-old woman with a history of treated ADHD who reported stress related to work and a recent marriage, began treatment with the psychiatrist in July 2020; he diagnosed ADHD and prescribed Adderall 20 mg. She was seen by phone, video, and in person through December 2022, and over that time discussed marital difficulties and separation from her husband. According to the Accusation, during multiple visits she asked for his private email address and made flirtatious comments (including that she fantasized about being with a doctor and suggesting a sexualized nickname for him); at one visit she tried to sit on his lap; and at another she intentionally exposed her breasts, to which he responded "those are nice." On or about August 31, 2022, during a clinical visit, he and the patient exchanged sexually explicit emails. He documented none of these events, did not refer her elsewhere, and continued treating her.

The matter surfaced when the patient's husband saw the email exchange and complained to the psychiatrist's employer. At a December 2022 visit the psychiatrist charted only that the husband was accusing her of liking her doctors, and then recommended she transfer to a female psychiatrist and seek psychotherapy. The Accusation charged sexual misconduct with a patient, gross negligence through multiple inappropriate sexual interactions, and failure to maintain adequate records. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist admitted only that a prima facie case could be established; no findings were made.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with patient disclosure of probation status, 40 hours/year education, medical record keeping course, professionalism program (ethics course), professional boundaries program, psychiatric evaluation, psychotherapy, practice monitor, solo practice prohibition, third-party chaperone for female patients; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery of $24,869.00.

narrative: The psychiatrist, licensed since 1990 and whose license had expired unrenewed in 2021 after he retired, surrendered it without admitting the charges, agreeing only that the Board could establish a factual basis for the Accusation's charges of gross negligence and general unprofessional conduct.

According to the Accusation, the psychiatrist had treated Patient A, an adult man with paranoid schizophrenia, for at least a decade in a hospital-employed position, including regular alprazolam prescriptions from about 2017 to 2020. By 2020 the patient was significantly impaired and unable to care for himself; his wife was his caregiver and accompanied him to appointments, and in March 2020 the psychiatrist noted that she had been told she would need to seek a conservatorship because he was gravely disabled. While still treating Patient A, the psychiatrist became romantically and sexually involved with the wife (in 2020 by his account, or late 2019 by hers). In August 2020 he self-reported the relationship to his employer, which opened an investigation, informed the patient, and transferred his care to another physician; the psychiatrist retired days later. In a 2024 Board interview he admitted the sexual relationship. The Accusation, citing APA and AMA ethics guidance on romantic or sexual relationships with key third parties, alleged that a sexual relationship with the spouse and caregiver of a current patient was an extreme departure from the standard of care.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; costs of $47,002 payable before any new or reinstated license; any reapplication treated as a petition for reinstatement with the Accusation's allegations deemed admitted.

narrative: According to the Accusation, the psychiatrist, in solo private practice, began treating a patient in 2007 in connection with a workers' compensation claim for severe anxiety, possible PTSD, and selective mutism, and provided psychotherapy until about 2018. When the patient became embroiled in civil litigation with her neighbors, the psychiatrist signed numerous declarations under penalty of perjury in the patient's support (2017-2018), identifying herself as the patient's doctor and asserting as fact that the neighbors had harassed, bullied, sexually harassed, and illegally recorded the patient, that they had caused the patient's anxiety disorders and were liable for future treatment estimated at about $68,000, and offering opinions that particular neighbors were not credible, had a history of drug use, or were paranoid, although she had never examined them. She attached her bills for the patient's care, including a $7,900 bill for "room and board" when the patient stayed in her home, and sent a letter to opposing counsel claiming power of attorney to speak for the patient. The Accusation alleged that she acknowledged the patient wrote the declarations and that she signed them without knowing whether the contents were true, because she thought it would help the patient's case, and that she had a friendship with the patient alongside treatment: they traveled together (including to visit her family out of state), dined and shopped together, and each stayed in the other's home. She produced a certification that she had no medical records for the patient.

The Accusation charged gross negligence and repeated negligent acts for crossing doctor-patient boundaries and for submitting declarations presenting a patient's accounts and opinions about unexamined third parties as fact, plus inadequate records. It also cited prior discipline in 2012 (stayed revocation with probation) for false statements in a workers' compensation psychiatric report and billing and a misdemeanor conviction for prescribing hydrocodone by fraud. The psychiatrist surrendered her license, agreeing that the complainant could establish a factual basis for the charges; no findings were made.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; any future petition for reinstatement to be treated as a petition for reinstatement of a revoked or surrendered license, with all Accusation allegations deemed true.

narrative: The psychiatrist began treating Patient 1, a 29-year-old woman, in October 2014 for psychiatric symptoms following a motor vehicle accident, including anxiety, insomnia, fatigue, cognitive complaints, and back and neck pain, with a significant family psychiatric and substance-use history. According to the Accusation, he prescribed zolpidem regularly from June 2015 to March 2022, at average daily doses in 2016 (22.6 mg) and later years above the recommended maximum, and alprazolam regularly from February 2016 to March 2022, with average doses ranging from about 2 mg to 9 mg per day. CURES showed several early refills only five to six days after prior fills in late 2018 and early 2019, yet the records indicated he did not query CURES until March 2020, despite the mandate that took effect in October 2018, and then not again until December 2021.

The Accusation further alleged that in November 2018, while still treating Patient 1 and prescribing her alprazolam and zolpidem, the psychiatrist purchased a home jointly with her (by his account, he paid 80 percent and she 20 percent), compromising his objectivity and effectiveness as her psychiatrist. These were charged as repeated negligent acts: failure to properly monitor controlled-substance treatment and entering a joint real-estate purchase with an active patient. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist did not admit the allegations but agreed that the Board could establish a factual basis for them and gave up his right to contest them. The public reprimand was expressly issued for an improper business transaction with a patient and inappropriate monitoring after prescribing controlled substances.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; education course (40 hours); cost recovery of $12,861.57.

narrative: The psychiatrist worked as a child and adolescent psychiatrist, in part for an organization providing mental health treatment to youth in foster care. According to the Accusation, Patient 1 began treatment with him at age 14 in 2017; she had a history of neglect, sexual abuse, and trauma by caregivers, and was diagnosed with ADHD and oppositional defiant disorder (rule out bipolar disorder and PTSD). He continued prescribing for her after she turned 18. He allegedly texted her on his personal cell phone, remarked that he might have to come over and spank her when she forgot her medication, took her to a birthday dinner, bought gifts for her and her child, and followed her on social media. In June 2021 he arranged a Sunday "appointment" outside the office: he picked her up, hugged her, took her to lunch and a shopping center he frequented personally, held her hand, repeatedly touched her lower back, said he wanted to spoil her, and ended by having her join him in the back seat of his car, where she lay in his lap while he massaged her shoulders, head, and face. His chart note described only medication issues. The patient texted him that she felt uncomfortable and ended treatment with him. He told investigators the touching was supportive and therapeutic and denied many of her allegations.

The Accusation also alleged that over about five years beginning in 2015 he treated Patient 2, a teenage foster youth with a history of sexual abuse and suicidal behavior, while texting her on his personal phone, including her in outings with his family, and giving her gifts (including an emotional support dog), continuing after agency staff counseled him about boundaries in 2018. The charges were gross negligence (boundary and ethics violations) and repeated negligent acts; no sexual misconduct offense was charged. The case was resolved by stipulated settlement in which the psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 7 years' probation with 90 days' actual suspension, 40 hours/year of education in boundaries/professionalism, professionalism (ethics) program, professional boundaries program before resuming practice, practice monitor; solo practice prohibited; telehealth only (no in-person practice) and no treatment of female patients, with required patient notification log; prohibited from supervising PAs/advanced practice nurses; cost recovery of $66,389.75.

narrative: The psychiatrist, a board-certified geriatric psychiatrist employed as a staff psychiatrist in a state correctional psychiatric inpatient program who also had a part-time private geriatric practice, was the subject of an Accusation based on a misdemeanor criminal conviction. After a hearing, an administrative law judge found that in 2018 police responded to a domestic violence call at the psychiatrist's home after his wife reported that he had pushed her down a flight of stairs during an argument about her plan to travel abroad with their toddler; officers observed abrasions on her shins. The psychiatrist first told officers he had not touched her and that she slipped, then admitted he had touched or tapped her shoulder while telling her to get out, but denied that this caused the fall. He was arrested, charged with felony corporal injury to a spouse, and pled no contest to misdemeanor battery on a spouse; he was placed on three years of court probation with a work-alternative program, community service, a 52-week anger management course, and fines. In a later Board interview he again initially attributed the fall to his wife's emotional state before acknowledging touching her.

The judge found that the battery and the inconsistent statements about his culpability constituted unprofessional conduct and that the conviction was substantially related to the duties of a physician, rejecting the argument that it was a purely personal matter. In mitigation, the judge found that he had completed the anger management course, stress management, couples counseling, and an ethics and professionalism course, had complied with criminal probation, had excellent work evaluations with no evidence of misconduct at work, and had a single conviction. The judge found a deviation from the disciplinary guidelines (which call for at least stayed revocation and five years' probation) warranted.
cases.outcome: Public reproval (public reprimand); no probation imposed.

narrative: The psychiatrist was charged in an Accusation with dangerous use of alcohol, a substantially related criminal conviction, and general unprofessional conduct arising from a 2017 single-vehicle crash; in the stipulated settlement he admitted the truth of every charge and allegation. According to the Accusation, at about 1:40 a.m. highway patrol officers found his car against a large pole at a freeway off-ramp with major front-end damage and deployed airbags. A passenger said they had been driving home from a bar or nightclub. The psychiatrist had red, watery eyes, slurred speech, and a strong odor of alcohol; he admitted driving and drinking two 16-ounce beers, failed field sobriety tests, and gave breath samples of about 0.13%. He was arrested, and a blood sample drawn shortly afterward measured 0.175%. He was found to have a broken back and underwent surgery the next day; the car was totaled.

He was charged with misdemeanor driving under the influence and driving with a blood alcohol level of 0.08% or more, with an enhancement allegation of 0.15% or more, and in 2019 pleaded no contest to driving at 0.08% or above. He was sentenced to four days in jail, three years of court probation, a three-month DUI program, and fines. In a 2020 Board interview he acknowledged having had a glass of wine at dinner and about two to three beers and a Jell-O shot at the bar in the hours before the crash.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with abstention from alcohol and controlled substances, biological fluid testing, professionalism (ethics) program, psychiatric evaluation, psychotherapy if recommended, and probation monitoring costs.

narrative: After a hearing at which the psychiatrist did not appear (he was incarcerated and his attorney declined to attend), an administrative law judge found that in 2021 he was convicted in federal court, on his guilty plea to one count of a 23-count indictment, of illegally importing a firearm, specifically a silencer shipped in packaging labeled as a motorcycle fuel filter. In his plea agreement he admitted importing at least 13 firearms into the country by similar methods. He was sentenced to 18 months in prison and a $10,000 fine, with a mental health evaluation, evaluation for residential drug treatment, and three years of supervised release requiring drug testing, substance abuse treatment, alcohol abstinence, and mental health treatment. His license had been suspended in late 2021 because of the conviction. The First Amended Accusation further alleged that federal agents searching his homes had found 13 suppressors, 18 firearms (some loaded, including assault weapons), and a substance that field-tested positive for methamphetamine next to a handgun and rifle.

The judge also found that, during the Board investigation that began with a 2020 complaint, he agreed to physical and psychiatric examinations. He reported taking buprenorphine for chronic back pain and Adderall without an ADHD diagnosis, yet his witnessed urine screen was negative for both. The Board's psychiatric evaluator concluded that his trauma history and stressors required monitoring, a year of weekly psychotherapy, substance abuse treatment, random drug screens, and second opinions on the need for Adderall and opioids. The judge found cause for discipline both for a substantially related conviction and because his psychological condition required restrictions to practice safely, and, with no mitigation or rehabilitation evidence presented, concluded that public protection required revocation.
cases.outcome: License revoked; payment of $4,446.25 in investigation and prosecution costs is a condition of any reinstatement.

narrative: The psychiatrist, licensed since 1998 and representing himself, admitted the truth of every charge and allegation in the Accusation and surrendered his license. The Accusation alleged that he owned and operated a drug treatment center offering detoxification, partial hospitalization, intensive outpatient, and outpatient services. In September 2020 he waived indictment and pleaded guilty in federal court to a felony count of conspiracy to pay illegal remunerations for referrals to recovery homes. In May 2022 he was sentenced to 15 months in federal prison and three years' supervised release and ordered to pay $493,104.35 in restitution; he reported to prison in August 2022. He did not report the felony charge or conviction to the Board within 30 days as required.

The Accusation also described two drunk-driving arrests. In April 2020 highway patrol stopped him for driving about 90 mph in a 65 mph zone; he admitted drinking, failed field sobriety tests, and had breath alcohol results of 0.15 and 0.16 percent. In February 2021 a witness identified him as the driver who struck a parked car outside a hotel and left; officers found him in the lobby smelling of alcohol and unsteady, and he could not complete sobriety tests and refused breath and chemical testing. In October 2021 he was convicted of misdemeanor DUI offenses arising from both arrests and placed on five years' summary probation. The Accusation noted a 2010 DUI conviction, a 2015 reckless driving conviction, and a 2018 Board public reprimand for alcohol use, a substantially related conviction, and unprofessional conduct.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; costs of $8,459.25 payable before any new or reinstated license; allegations deemed admitted in any reinstatement petition or other California health licensing application.

narrative: An administrative law judge found, after a contested hearing, that the psychiatrist, licensed in late 2019 and then a psychiatry resident, was convicted on a nolo contendere plea of misdemeanor driving with a blood alcohol content of 0.08 percent or more. In June 2021, after a morning shift, he attended a party hosted by an attending physician, drank several glasses of champagne without food, and drove home alone. Feeling impaired, he tried to exit the freeway but lost control of the car and struck a concrete divider on the off-ramp. Responding police noted an odor of alcohol and red, watery eyes; he performed poorly on field sobriety tests, and breath tests about 90 minutes later showed a blood alcohol content of about 0.19 percent. He admitted at hearing that he had not been candid with the officer, saying he had drunk one hard seltzer. The court imposed 36 months' summary probation, fines, a first-offender alcohol program, and a victim impact program, all of which he completed. The judge found cause for discipline for a substantially related conviction, use of alcohol in a manner dangerous to himself and the public, and unprofessional conduct.

The judge also found substantial rehabilitation: an addiction medicine evaluation concluded he did not have an alcohol use disorder, he had abstained since the arrest with 335 negative monitored breath tests, he attended AA and therapy, and supervisors and colleagues testified to his clinical skill and the absence of any alcohol concerns at work. Because he rebutted the presumption that he was a substance-abusing licensee, the judge concluded that probation would be unduly harsh and that a public reprimand was sufficient. Costs were reduced by 75 percent in light of his income and student debt.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; cost recovery of $4,345 (reduced from $17,383.75) payable within six months.

narrative: According to the Accusation, in March 2021 police saw a car driven by the psychiatrist going the wrong way on a one-way street at high speed and running stop signs. Officers lost sight of it, then found it parked with two passengers inside and the driver's seat empty; the passengers said the driver had parked and fled on foot. The psychiatrist returned soon afterward, said he had been driving, and denied drinking. Officers noted the odor of alcohol, watery and unfocused eyes, slurred speech, and an unsteady gait. He performed poorly on field sobriety tests, would not blow into the preliminary alcohol screening device, and was arrested. At the hospital where a warrant-authorized blood draw was attempted, he repeatedly pulled the needle out, flailed, and yelled, and staff could not obtain blood after three attempts. At the jail he cried and made threats against himself, and was placed in a padded safety cell.

He was charged with misdemeanor DUI and with resisting or obstructing an officer. In March 2022 he pleaded no contest to DUI, with a stipulated blood alcohol concentration of 0.08%; the resisting count was dropped. He was sentenced to three years' supervised probation, two days in jail, a three-month alcohol education program, and fines. The Accusation charged conviction of a substantially related crime, use of alcohol in a manner dangerous to himself and the public, and unprofessional conduct. In the stipulated settlement he did not contest that the complainant could establish a prima facie case; he made no admissions and no findings were made.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with abstinence from controlled substances and alcohol, biological fluid testing, professionalism (ethics) program, notification of hospitals/facilities/insurers, and prohibition on supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery $10,045.00.

narrative: According to the Accusation, on a November 2021 afternoon (about 3:15 p.m.) the psychiatrist was in a motor vehicle collision while under the influence of alcohol, and the other driver was injured. He was arrested at the scene for DUI causing injury. About three and a half hours later, two breath tests at the detention center showed blood alcohol concentrations of 0.26% and 0.263%, more than three times the legal limit. He was released the next day.

In March 2022 the prosecutor filed misdemeanor charges of driving under the influence and driving with a blood alcohol level of 0.08% or more. In April 2022 he pleaded no contest to the 0.08% count and was placed on three years' summary probation with 180 hours of community service and a nine-month first-offender alcohol and drug education and counseling program. The Accusation charged conviction of a substantially related crime and use of alcohol in a manner dangerous to himself or others, or impairing his ability to practice safely. It did not describe his practice or any patient care issue. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist admitted the truth of every charge and allegation in the Accusation.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 4 years' probation with waiver of right to seek early termination, abstinence from controlled substances and alcohol, psychotherapy, notice to employers/supervisors, biological fluid testing, substance abuse support group meetings, worksite monitor, notification of hospitals/facilities/insurers, and prohibition on supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery $14,400.50.

narrative: In October 2022, at about 11 p.m., highway patrol officers responded to a witness report of a possibly impaired driver who had been drifting between freeway lanes, nearly stopping on a freeway transition with no traffic ahead, forcing other drivers to brake or swerve, and nearly hitting another car after exiting. Officers located the vehicle weaving and straddling the double yellow line and stopped it; the driver was the psychiatrist. He had red, watery eyes, a strong odor of alcohol came from the vehicle, he walked with an unsteady gait, admitted drinking beer earlier, and failed field sobriety tests. He refused voluntary breath or blood testing, and a warrant blood draw taken about three hours after the witness's observations showed a blood alcohol concentration of 0.29 percent. In June 2023 he pleaded no contest to a misdemeanor count of driving with a blood alcohol level of 0.08 percent or more and was sentenced to three years' summary probation, including a nine-month first-offender alcohol and drug program and a hospital-and-morgue program.

The Accusation charged conviction of a substantially related crime, use of alcohol in a manner dangerous to himself or the public, and unprofessional conduct. No patient care was implicated. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist admitted the truth of each charge and allegation in the Accusation.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with abstention from controlled substances and alcohol, biological fluid testing, substance abuse support group meetings, worksite monitor, psychiatric evaluation, psychotherapy, professionalism (ethics) program, 100 hours of free community service, employer notification; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery of $17,504.00.

narrative: This case arose from a criminal prosecution in a California superior court. According to the Accusation, in August 2022 the psychiatrist was convicted of two misdemeanors: prescribing, dispensing, or furnishing dangerous drugs without an appropriate prior examination and a medical indication, and failing to maintain adequate and accurate records relating to the provision of services to patients. The Board charged the psychiatrist with conviction of crimes substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of a physician, conviction of a statute regulating dangerous drugs or controlled substances, and violation of the Medical Practice Act. The Accusation describes only the convictions themselves; it does not identify the patients, medications, or circumstances underlying the criminal case.
In the stipulated settlement, the psychiatrist admitted the truth of each and every charge and allegation in the Accusation.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; two years' probation with 40 hours/year of education courses, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, and practice monitor (or professional enhancement program); cost recovery of $15,452.00.

narrative: According to the Second Amended Accusation, in October 2022 the psychiatrist sideswiped the concrete center-median wall of a highway while driving home in the evening. A highway patrol officer responding to the crash noted a strong odor of alcohol; the psychiatrist said another car had cut him off and denied drinking, but he had an unsteady gait, stumbled on the walk-and-turn, and was unable to complete field sobriety tests. He was arrested, and two breath tests showed blood alcohol concentrations of 0.19% and 0.18%. He was charged with misdemeanor driving under the influence and driving with a blood alcohol level of 0.08% or higher, with an excessive-blood-alcohol enhancement, and in January 2024 he pleaded no contest to the 0.08% count. The criminal court imposed three years' probation, a three-month first-offender DUI program, an ignition interlock device, and fines. No patient care issues were alleged.

The Second Amended Accusation charged conviction of a substantially related offense and use of alcohol in a manner dangerous to himself or others. The matter was resolved by stipulated settlement in which the psychiatrist did not admit the allegations but agreed that the Board could establish a factual basis for the charges at a hearing.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with abstention from alcohol and controlled substances, random biological fluid testing, professionalism (ethics) program, psychiatric evaluation, psychotherapy, medical evaluation and treatment; prohibited from supervising PAs/advanced practice nurses; cost recovery of $18,289.80.

narrative: In October 2019, while living out of state, the psychiatrist was stopped by police for driving erratically at up to 105 miles per hour on an interstate highway; when the officer approached, she sped off and reached about 115 miles per hour before the officer ended the pursuit. Warrants issued for this and a similar incident two days earlier. After being taken into custody she was ordered to undergo a competency evaluation and was hospitalized at a state psychiatric hospital for about three weeks, where on admission she claimed hit men were trying to kill her; she was diagnosed with bipolar I disorder, recent manic episode, and found competent to stand trial. In August 2020 she was found guilty after a bench trial of two counts of felony eluding and two counts of misdemeanor reckless driving. The Board's license had already been suspended by an interim suspension order in January 2021.

At the Board's request, a psychiatrist evaluator reviewed complaints to the Board, a prior employer's reports of unusual behavior, court records, and hospital records, and interviewed her by videoconference in October 2020. He found her restless, not always rational, and delusional (she explained the speeding by saying a police officer was trying to kill her), with severely impaired judgment: she did not acknowledge boundary violations in allowing a patient she was treating to live on her boat and dine at her house, insisted she had to keep treating a patient after realizing she had a prior sexual relationship with him, and rejected psychiatric treatment for herself. He diagnosed bipolar I disorder, presently hypomanic, and narcissistic personality disorder, and concluded there were no terms under which she could safely practice. She did not file a notice of defense, and the Board, acting by default, found all allegations of the Accusation true: mental illness affecting her ability to practice safely, conviction of substantially related crimes, and unprofessional conduct.
cases.outcome: License revoked (default decision); any reapplication to be treated as a petition for reinstatement.

narrative: The physician, who had psychiatry/addiction training and a long history of opioid addiction, worked full time at an urgent care clinic while also treating his own cash-only psychiatric and Suboxone patients there. A 2018 complaint from a nurse practitioner alleged that he threatened staff with a firearm, bullied staff, and was impaired on duty; according to the Accusation, coworkers described him carrying a handgun at work, drinking from a flask, and once placing a gun on his desk and making a threatening remark. The administrative law judge found that two urine tests (2018 and 2019) were positive for buprenorphine, and the first also for clonazepam, alcohol, and cannabis, with no matching active prescriptions in CURES; loose pills were found on him during a 2019 search. He admitted obtaining his own buprenorphine for years from an out-of-state prescriber under an assumed name, paying cash, and treating 35 to 40 Suboxone patients. He had prior discipline in two other states, including a guilty plea to narcotic possession after obtaining Demerol through his position as a county medical examiner, and an indefinite suspension after prescribing Suboxone to his partner and diverting it.

After a three-day hearing, the judge found the Board's evaluating psychiatrist persuasive and unrebutted: she diagnosed severe opioid use disorder, mild alcohol use disorder, cannabis use disorder, and antisocial personality disorder, citing deceit, lack of insight, prescribing controlled substances to his partner and diverting the partner's clonazepam, socializing with addiction patients, keeping their charts unsecured, and practicing outside his training. He denied current substance abuse and disputed the diagnoses. The judge found by clear and convincing evidence that his ability to practice safely was impaired by mental illness and that his use of controlled substances was dangerous and impaired his practice; he was already under an interim suspension order.
cases.outcome: License revoked.

narrative: According to the Accusation, in October 2019 the psychiatrist saw a child for psychiatric treatment, accompanied by his mother, and arrived late with heavy-lidded eyes and slurred speech, was significantly confused about the patient's condition (referring to the child by the wrong gender and discussing the efficacy of a medication he was not taking), and the mother reported that she was under the influence. Two months earlier she had been arrested for driving under the influence after poor driving; her blood tested positive for multiple controlled substances, two of which she had prescribed to other members of her household, and bottles of controlled substances she had prescribed to her husband were found in her car, although she admitted to police taking only one medication. CURES data for 2017-2020 showed she prescribed to an employee and relatives the same substances found in her blood, and multiple pharmacies raised concerns about her co-prescribing of opioids and benzodiazepines and prescribing to family members; at least one refused to fill her future prescriptions. In her Board interview she denied illicit or recreational drug use and disclosed no substance treatment.

A Board-appointed psychiatrist noted that she prescribed large amounts of controlled substances to family members and an employee for the same drugs she used, received prescriptions for many of the same opioids and benzodiazepines herself, sought unauthorized refills, used medications without appropriate medical oversight, and lacked insight; the evaluator diagnosed opioid use disorder and sedative, hypnotic, or anxiolytic use disorder that, untreated, impaired her ability to practice safely. The Accusation charged impairment, dangerous use of drugs, dishonest false statements to the Board investigator, and practicing while impaired. Her license was already under an interim suspension order. She did not admit the allegations but agreed that the Board could establish a factual basis for the charges and surrendered her license.
cases.outcome: License surrendered; may not petition for reinstatement for two years, and the Accusation's allegations will be deemed admitted in any reinstatement or future licensing proceeding.

narrative: The Accusation in this case is brief and was brought solely as an action for mental impairment. According to the Accusation, during a Board investigation (whose origin is not described) the psychiatrist voluntarily underwent a psychiatric evaluation by a Board-approved evaluator, who reviewed her mental health records and investigation materials and examined her in person. In a June 2020 report, the evaluator opined that she suffers from a mental illness that impairs her ability to practice safely and that she was then unable to practice safely: she was only beginning to be stabilized and treated for an illness she had most likely had for several years, if not most of her adult life. During the evaluation she admitted to having an inappropriate relationship with a patient, among other admissions related to her mental health. The evaluator found that she did not understand doctor-patient boundaries, which could seriously affect a psychiatric patient's mental condition, and concluded that she needed ongoing psychiatric treatment and psychotropic medication, monitoring by a psychiatrist for depression and anxiety in addition to her bipolar disorder, and courses on HIPAA, boundary violations, and ethics. The Accusation does not describe the nature of the relationship with the patient.
The psychiatrist did not admit the allegations; she agreed that a prima facie case could be established at hearing and gave up her right to contest the charges.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with 40 hours/year education (HIPAA, professional boundaries, ethics), professionalism program, professional boundaries program (no practice until completed), psychiatric evaluation (no practice until found mentally fit), psychotherapy, practice monitor, prohibition on supervising PAs/APNs, and probation monitoring costs.

narrative: The Accusation alleged that the psychiatrist, licensed since 1974, might be unable to practice medicine safely because of a medical condition. In August 2021 the Board received a complaint that the psychiatrist might be suffering from a medical condition affecting the ability to practice safely, and in January 2022 the psychiatrist asked the Board to accept surrender of the license, which had expired at the end of 2021 and had not been renewed. The document does not describe the nature of the condition or any patient care issue.

In the stipulated surrender, the psychiatrist admitted the truth of each charge and allegation in the Accusation (that is, the inability to practice safely due to a medical condition) and surrendered the license.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; costs of $1,118.75 payable before any new or reinstated license; any reapplication treated as a petition for reinstatement with the Accusation's allegations deemed admitted.

narrative: This was not a disciplinary action against an existing license but a Stipulation for a Probationary License with a physician applying for an initial California physician's and surgeon's license. The applicant had submitted the application in January 2022 and reported to the Board that he had taken a leave of absence from training. The stipulation does not describe the underlying events. It states only that the Board may act where an applicant's ability to practice safely is impaired by mental illness, for unprofessional conduct, and for use of dangerous drugs or alcohol in a manner dangerous to the licensee or others, and that these grounds supported denial of the license. Instead of denying the application, the Board's Chief of Licensing and the applicant agreed that a license would be issued on probation. The applicant waived a Statement of Issues and hearing. No findings were made and nothing was admitted beyond the stipulation itself.

The probation terms show that the Board's concern was substance use and mental health. They include random observed biological fluid testing, weekly substance abuse support group meetings, a worksite monitor for a substance-abusing licensee, complete abstinence from controlled substances and alcohol, and ongoing psychotherapy with quarterly reports. The applicant was allowed to start at the second-year testing frequency because he had met the regulatory criteria for previous testing and sobriety.
cases.outcome: Probationary license issued; three years' probation with biological fluid testing, weekly substance abuse support group meetings, worksite monitor, abstinence from controlled substances and alcohol, psychotherapy, solo practice prohibition, notification of employers/hospitals/insurers, and prohibition on supervising PAs and advanced practice nurses.

narrative: The psychiatrist surrendered his license to resolve an Accusation alleging that he could not practice safely because of a mental or physical illness affecting competency. He agreed that the Board could establish a factual basis for the charge but did not admit it. According to the Accusation, he was in a motorized bicycle accident in July 2019 and suffered multiple traumatic injuries requiring hospitalization, and he had a stroke while in the hospital. About three weeks later the Board received an anonymous complaint that he was incapacitated and that his medical corporation was operating without a current medical director. He was interviewed and voluntarily agreed to an evaluation.

In May 2021 a clinical neuropsychologist performed a full neuropsychological evaluation and diagnosed major vascular neurocognitive disorder secondary to the stroke. The impairments were in the moderate to severe range and included loss of executive functions such as sustained attention and concentration, new learning, sequencing, visual scanning, and abstract thinking, along with distractibility. The neuropsychologist concluded that he was not able to practice medicine safely. The Accusation alleged no patient-care deficiencies; the only ground was impairment from illness.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; costs of $7,991.25 payable before any new or reinstated license; any reapplication treated as a petition for reinstatement with the Accusation's allegations deemed admitted.

narrative: This decision granted a petition for reinstatement after a hearing, and the administrative law judge's findings describe the history. The psychiatrist had a solo private practice and hospital staff work. He had depression and misused controlled substances, mainly stimulants, from his residency in the mid-1990s. The judge found that he snorted crushed Adderall and Ritalin tablets that patients had returned to him. After residential treatment in 2007 and about five years of sobriety, he relapsed. In May 2014 his nurse practitioner found him passed out in the office after he took stimulants and then Saphris to counteract them, and she reported him to the Board. A 2015 Accusation for dangerous use of controlled substances was settled with five years' probation starting March 2016. He then failed to report for testing, tested positive for a controlled substance, and did not cooperate with the testing program. These violations led to two cease-practice orders and a petition to revoke probation, and he surrendered his license in July 2017.

The judge also found that a January 2017 altercation with a former girlfriend led to a no-contest plea to misdemeanor domestic battery. He violated that criminal probation by using alcohol and drugs in December 2017; the conviction was later dismissed. In treatment after that incident, a sex and love addiction was identified as driving his relapses. The judge found him sober since January 2018, with negative tests apart from one in January 2018, and active in AA. He had opened a substance-abuse treatment center in which he did not act as a physician. The judge concluded that he had shown rehabilitation by clear and convincing evidence. Because of his relapses and earlier failure on probation, the judge required a long probation, a psychiatric evaluation before practice, and a solo-practice prohibition.
cases.outcome: License reinstated, immediately revoked, revocation stayed; seven years' probation with psychiatric evaluation before resuming practice, abstinence from controlled substances and alcohol, biological fluid testing, substance abuse support group meetings, worksite monitor, solo practice prohibition, professionalism (ethics) course, and prohibition on supervising PAs and advanced practice nurses.

narrative: The psychiatrist, licensed since 2011 and co-owner of a psychiatric group practice, did not contest that the Board could establish a prima facie case on the Accusation's charges of failing to comply with a Board-ordered mental and physical evaluation and of impairment due to mental illness affecting competency; she made no admissions.

According to the Accusation, the case began with her September 2022 arrest on felony charges of inflicting corporal injury on a spouse and making criminal threats; prosecutors ultimately did not file charges. The arrest report contained allegations that she had assaulted and threatened her husband, vandalized her in-laws' home, and threatened to kill herself; her husband told police that her mental health had declined rapidly after the birth of their third child, that she had been diagnosed with bipolar disorder and borderline personality and had stopped taking her escitalopram and lamotrigine, and he raised possible drug use and erratic behavior such as climbing onto the roof. After a Board investigator's interview in February 2023 she declined a voluntary mental and physical evaluation, and the Board ordered one in July 2023. At the medical evaluation she declined, citing protected health information, to disclose her medical history, medications, or drug and alcohol use, or to release records, so the examiner could not determine whether she had an impairing physical condition. The Board-appointed psychiatrist, also denied access to her records, found a picture consistent with compulsive personality type and a possible underlying mood, posttraumatic, anxiety, or adjustment disorder, and concluded she could not practice safely without restrictions, monitoring, and psychiatric care.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with professionalism (ethics) program, psychiatric evaluation and medical evaluation with no practice until found fit, psychotherapy, medical treatment as required, practice monitor (or professional enhancement program), notification of facilities/insurers; prohibited from directly supervising PAs/APNs; costs of $45,128.

narrative: The psychiatrist, licensed since 2011, settled the Accusation without admitting it, agreeing only that the Board could establish a prima facie case for impairment due to mental illness, dishonest or corrupt acts, and general unprofessional conduct. The charges arose from conduct outside clinical practice rather than patient care.

According to the Accusation, in January 2023 police investigating a residential burglary found that the psychiatrist had used a previously provided key to enter her ex-boyfriend's apartment and remove property; the next day she pulled a building fire alarm when he would not answer his phone. After Miranda warnings she admitted the entry, the taking of property, and the false alarm; stolen property was recovered from her car, and a felony first-degree burglary complaint was filed. Later that month she left a threatening voicemail for a local elected official and was placed on a 72-hour psychiatric hold after a disturbance that frightened a former employer; she had a prior bipolar disorder diagnosis with hospitalizations in 2013-2014, was diagnosed with bipolar I disorder, manic episode, and was discharged on lithium, aripiprazole, lamotrigine, and other medications. In February 2023 she left another threatening voicemail, was again hospitalized on a hold after a community disturbance, and on discharge (with residual grandiose delusions noted) was taken into custody, served with a restraining order, and later charged with two misdemeanor counts of annoying telephone calls. A Board-ordered psychiatric evaluation in July 2023 concluded that her ability to practice was impaired by bipolar I disorder and PTSD, citing periodic manic psychotic episodes with risk of loss of control. The Accusation does not state the outcome of the criminal charges.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with waiver of early termination, abstention from ketamine with biological fluid testing, professionalism (ethics) program, psychiatric evaluation, psychotherapy, biweekly psychiatric treatment with quarterly reports, notification of employers/insurers; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; costs of $46,952.

narrative: The psychiatrist, licensed since 1972, surrendered the license without admitting the charge, agreeing only that the Board could establish a factual basis for it. The Accusation, which contained a single cause for action, alleged only that the psychiatrist's ability to practice medicine safely was impaired because his competency had been affected by a mental condition, a physical condition, or both. The document gives no further details about the nature of the condition, how it came to the Board's attention, or any patient care.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; any reapplication treated as a petition for reinstatement with the Accusation's allegations deemed admitted. No cost recovery ordered.

narrative: According to the Accusation, in November 2016 the psychiatrist telephoned a community pharmacy with a prescription for an antibiotic and diazepam in the name of a fictitious patient, intending to obtain the medications for her own use. The pharmacist noticed that the "patient" had recently filled diazepam (making this an early refill) and, when the psychiatrist arrived to pick it up, recognized her voice as that of the prescribing doctor and refused to fill it. An altercation followed, and sheriff's deputies who located her nearby reported that she refused commands, pulled away and kicked during handcuffing, kicked the patrol-car window, and showed poor balance, slurred speech, dilated pupils, and droopy eyelids; a blood sample drawn the next morning was positive for opiates and benzodiazepines. The Accusation further alleged that over roughly nineteen months (April 2015 to November 2016) she wrote about 19 prescriptions to herself under variants of the fictitious name, including clonazepam, lorazepam, triazolam, phentermine, and zolpidem, with zolpidem quantities in early 2016 consistent with 20 mg per day, double the maximum recommended dose, without any documented justification. She also prescribed clonazepam, amphetamines, and zolpidem to Patient A, a former private-practice patient living abroad, while keeping no medical records for Patient A or for herself.

The Accusation charged that writing prescriptions in a false name, prolonged self-prescribing of controlled substances when other physicians were available, the absence of any records, and excessive dosing constituted gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, dishonest and corrupt acts, self-use of drugs in a dangerous manner, and inadequate records. The case was resolved by stipulated settlement in which the psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established; no findings were made.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with prohibition on ordering, prescribing, dispensing, or possessing controlled substances except as approved by another physician (worksite monitor may review), controlled substance log, abstention from controlled substances and alcohol, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, psychotherapy, biological fluid testing, worksite monitor, employer notification, and prohibition on supervising PAs/APRNs; probation monitoring costs.

narrative: According to the Accusation, from about January 2014 through December 2015 the psychiatrist treated two of her own family members and regularly prescribed them high amounts of opioids and benzodiazepines in combination. Patient A, a 69-year-old female relative, complained of pain and anxiety attributed to trauma from prior cancer treatment; CURES records showed recurring prescriptions for hydrocodone/acetaminophen, oxycodone/acetaminophen, promethazine with codeine, alprazolam (escalating from 0.5 mg to 1 mg, #90 monthly), and clonazepam. Patient B, a 49-year-old male relative with orthopedic knee pain, received hydrocodone/acetaminophen, buprenorphine/naloxone (8/2 mg, #90 monthly), alprazolam, clonazepam, zolpidem, and eszopiclone, often several of these concurrently. The Accusation alleged that for both relatives she failed to perform or document an adequate history and physical examination (including an orthopedic exam for Patient B) or a full mental status examination, did not coordinate care with the treating oncologist or orthopedist or consult pain management, did not review or document review of CURES, did not obtain a controlled-substance agreement, did not timely refer the patients to other providers, and practiced over an extended period in areas (oncology, orthopedics, pain management) for which she lacked adequate training.

The Accusation charged gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, violation of the Medical Practice Act, and general unprofessional conduct. The case was resolved by stipulated settlement in which the psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established on each charge; no findings were made.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with 40 hours/year of education courses, prescribing practices course, professionalism (ethics) program, psychiatric evaluation, practice monitor (or professional enhancement program), prohibition on prescribing controlled substances to family members or herself, and prohibition on supervising PAs/APRNs; probation monitoring costs.

narrative: According to the First Amended Accusation, the psychiatrist provided long-term outpatient care to three older women and prescribed benzodiazepines and other controlled substances for years without adequate examination, substance-use assessment, coordination with co-prescribers, or documentation. Patient 1, born in 1944 and treated since 1988 for anxiety, depression, and insomnia, received diazepam on 32 occasions and triazolam on 18 occasions between January 2011 and August 2013 without examination; refills were authorized after phone calls in which she reported being stable, and the faxed renewals were lost. He knew another physician was concurrently prescribing her hydrocodone/acetaminophen and methadone but never contacted that physician. In August 2013 he gave an early refill of diazepam 10 mg #120 with four refills; she died at home in October 2013 of acute mixed drug intoxication (methadone and benzodiazepines). Patient 2, a psychologist born in 1944 and treated since about 1995 for PTSD, depression, panic, and insomnia, received clonazepam for over 20 years plus phentermine and trazodone while drinking alcohol regularly, receiving opioids from an internist, and developing incontinence, word-finding difficulty, balance problems, and MRI findings consistent with dementia; he issued clonazepam and phentermine with multiple refills after a cancelled visit and first checked CURES in November 2018. Patient 3, born in 1941 with major depression, a history of opioid dependence, and a family history of alcohol use disorder, received methylphenidate, alprazolam, zolpidem, and other sedative-hypnotics, and benzodiazepines were continued after a November 2018 psychiatric hospitalization for suicidal ideation at which severe obstructive sleep apnea was diagnosed.

The Accusation charged prescribing without appropriate examination or indication, gross negligence, incompetence (including in dual-diagnosis care and psychopharmacology), repeated negligent acts, failure to document informed consent, and illegible, incomplete records. It noted prior Board probation imposed in 2002. The psychiatrist agreed in a stipulated settlement that a prima facie case could be established, without admitting the allegations; no findings were made.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with patient disclosure of probation status, 40 hours/year of education in psychopharmacology and neuroscience, medical record keeping course, practice monitor (or professional enhancement program), and prohibition on supervising PAs/APRNs; probation monitoring costs.

cases.type: Public reprimand / public letter of reprimand
narrative: According to the Board's Public Letter of Reprimand, an investigation by the Medical Board revealed that the psychiatrist did not follow the set requirements for dispensing controlled substances in an office setting, failed to discuss (or failed to document having discussed) the risks, benefits, and alternatives of psychotropic medications with patients or their guardians, and failed to obtain signed medication consent from patients or guardians. The letter characterizes these actions as violations of the medical records and unprofessional conduct provisions of the Business and Professions Code.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand; required to complete a prescribing practices course and a medical record keeping course.

narrative: The psychiatrist, a board-certified psychiatrist in long-standing solo private practice, had previously been on three years' Board probation (2016-2019) for prescribing large quantities of pain medications to an out-of-state family friend without an examination; that probation prohibited him from prescribing opiates. In January 2017, while on that probation, he prescribed hydrocodone-homatropine cough syrup to Patient 1, a long-time patient with schizophrenia who lacked a primary care physician, without a physical examination, calling it a 'bridge' and a 'minor lapse' and saying he did not connect that it violated his probation. In January 2019 he advised Patient 2 to taper off citalopram from 20 mg to 10 mg for a week and, to help, took a bottle from a cabinet of medications in his office that bore another patient's name label, told her the pills were expired but fine, and poured them into her pill dispenser, without documenting the dispensing. Uncomfortable, she did not take them and filed an online complaint with the Board. A 2020 search of his office found dozens of expired samples, some many years old, mixed with unexpired samples, and two expired medications prescribed to another patient.

After a hearing, an administrative law judge found, based on the persuasive and unrefuted opinion of the Board's psychiatrist expert, one simple departure (prescribing cough syrup without an examination) and three extreme departures: prescribing an opioid while prohibited by probation, dispensing expired medication returned by another patient, and failing to document the dispensing. The psychiatrist admitted the conduct but justified it as helping patients. The judge concluded that, despite prior probation and recent prescribing, recordkeeping, and professionalism courses, he showed a lax attitude toward prescribing, possessing, dispensing, and documenting medications and lacked insight, warranting five years' probation rather than the letter of reprimand he requested.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with controlled-substance record log and inventory access, 40 hours/year education, prescribing practices course, professionalism (ethics) program, clinical competence assessment followed by professional enhancement program, practice monitor, solo practice prohibition, prohibition on supervising PAs/APNs, and probation monitoring costs.

narrative: The psychiatrist was charged in an Accusation concerning three adult outpatients with opioid use disorder to whom he prescribed buprenorphine-naloxone (Suboxone) together with other controlled substances. According to the Accusation, Patient A, who also had ADHD and sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic dependence and had been in his care since 2008, received recurring prescriptions from 2014 onward for Suboxone, amphetamine salts, alprazolam, and diazepam, and for several months phenobarbital. Patient B, with anxiety and sedative dependence, received Suboxone, amphetamine salts, clonazepam, and diazepam from 2017 to 2020. Patient C, with anxiety, received Suboxone, diazepam, and alprazolam from 2017 to 2020. After California's mandatory CURES-consultation requirement took effect in October 2018, the Accusation alleged he did not check CURES at all for Patients A and C through March 2020, and checked it only once for Patient B.

The Accusation further alleged that his records were missing progress notes for multiple encounters with Patient A, did not document the basis for prescribing amphetamines, benzodiazepines, or Suboxone, did not document an ADHD assessment for Patient B, and contained inconsistent statements about patient evaluation. It charged gross negligence (inadequate records for Patients A and B; failure to review CURES for Patient C), repeated negligent acts, failure to consult CURES, and inadequate records. The Accusation did not separately allege that the prescribing itself was excessive. The psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established and made no admissions.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 4 years' probation with 40 hours/year of additional education, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, and practice monitor; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; probation monitoring costs.

narrative: The psychiatrist, in solo outpatient practice, was charged in an Accusation covering seven patients; he did not contest that the complainant could establish a factual basis for the charges and made no admissions. The central allegations concerned Patient A, a young woman recently out of residential substance-abuse treatment, whom he resumed seeing in 2017 and immediately prescribed Adderall XR 60 mg/day plus Xanax and bupropion without a history, mental status examination, ADHD evaluation, or prior records. According to the Accusation, the day after the first visit her mother reported an overdose with alcohol, cocaine use, and doctor-shopping; CURES showed Adderall from three other prescribers, yet he never checked CURES again or contacted the other prescribers. Over roughly two years, while the mother and a therapist sent repeated reports of whole bottles of Xanax and Adderall consumed, Klonopin taken with alcohol, a drug-induced psychosis, psychiatric hospitalization, police involvement, self-harm, and binge-purging, he did not respond or document any review, and continued, at times escalated, stimulants (up to 75 mg/day of Adderall XR, later Vyvanse 70 mg), benzodiazepines, and bupropion despite the seizure risk. Many progress notes were blank or a few words long.

Similar patterns were alleged for other patients: multiple concurrent benzodiazepines for a man also receiving opioids from his primary care physician (who later died of a cardiac dysrhythmia), benzodiazepines, stimulants, and hydrocodone without documented rationale for a patient with alcohol use disorder, high-dose Adderall with escalating Xanax and temazepam for a patient with insomnia, and about 20 blank progress notes for one patient. He was also alleged to have prescribed Adderall, Vyvanse, and Strattera for years to two of his own children without any evaluation or records. He told the Board investigator he was unfamiliar with the CURES-review requirement and did not always check it.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with proof of CURES registration, additional education course, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, and practice monitor; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; probation monitoring costs.

narrative: The psychiatrist, in private practice, was charged in an Accusation concerning two patients; he did not contest that a prima facie case could be established and made no admissions. According to the Accusation, Patient A, a woman with depression, fibromyalgia-related chronic pain and gastrointestinal disease, was receiving opioids from a neurologist; when the neurologist stopped practicing in 2015, the psychiatrist took over without a pain assessment, physical examination, prior records, or pain agreement. Over about three and a half years he prescribed oxycodone 10 mg at roughly 240 to 279 tablets a month (after earlier fentanyl and OxyContin), plus Klonopin and Zanaflex. He kept prescribing despite repeated insurer notices of early refills, CURES fills from other prescribers, a reported theft, prescriptions handed to her spouse when she was not present, a hospitalization for delirium and hypotension, and reduced kidney function, with no documented discussion of opioid-benzodiazepine risk or naloxone; he ended care only after CURES showed opioids from another prescriber. The Accusation alleged resulting harm including sedation, cognitive decline, colitis flares, hypotension with syncope, and opioid-induced hyperalgesia.

For Patient B, who had bipolar disorder, PTSD, dissociative identity disorder and borderline personality disorder, the Accusation alleged he prescribed about 75 mg/day of Adderall XR and 4 to 6 mg/day of Klonopin from 2015 to 2018, raised Klonopin in response to PTSD symptoms, did not check CURES, and did not consider whether the stimulant was causing her insomnia. When she called in 2017 agitated and suicidal, he prescribed olanzapine by phone without a documented suicide risk assessment or timely follow-up. Records for both patients repeatedly lacked mental status examinations, diagnoses, and treatment plans.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with 30 hours/year of additional education, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, and practice monitor (or professional enhancement program); prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; probation monitoring costs.

narrative: The psychiatrist did not contest that the Board could establish a prima facie case on the Accusation, which alleged gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, inadequate records, and unprofessional conduct in the long-term outpatient care of two patients, largely between 2014 and 2019. Patient 1, a woman treated for depression, possible bipolar disorder, and panic disorder with a past history of cocaine use, was prescribed alprazolam, later clonazepam (up to 4 mg/day), and carisoprodol, a muscle relaxant the Accusation said had no psychiatric indication, with no documented informed consent and no contact with her psychologist or other treaters. According to the Accusation, she attempted suicide by alprazolam overdose in 2014, was detoxified from clonazepam and carisoprodol in 2017, and developed delirium in 2018 before a month-long residential detoxification and a diagnosis of sedative, hypnotic, or anxiolytic use disorder. Despite this history, the psychiatrist resumed clonazepam (eventually up to three times daily) and added suvorexant in 2019. On two occasions in 2017, when told by phone that she was oversedated, slurring, confused, or possibly hallucinating, he advised medication changes rather than ensuring emergency evaluation.

Patient 2 had been treated since 2001 with an ADHD diagnosis that the Accusation alleged lacked a clinical basis, while his depression, anxiety, and insomnia went unaddressed; he received amphetamine products together with alprazolam at doses up to 1 mg four times daily (90-day supplies of 360 tablets), plus antipsychotics without stated indication, despite falls, balance problems, and a pharmacy warning about excessive sedative use. Records for both patients were described as inconsistent and nonchronological, with handwritten notes on medication lists and memo pads, unsigned or misdated entries, missing pages, two differing "certified" versions of one chart, and an after-the-fact summary apparently meant to support the ADHD diagnosis in a disability claim.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 4 years' probation with 40 hours/year education course, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, and practice monitor; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery $4,227.50.

narrative: The psychiatrist gave up the right to contest that the Board could establish a prima facie case on the First Amended Accusation, which alleged gross negligence (two patients), repeated negligent acts, clearly excessive prescribing, and inadequate records in the outpatient care of three patients between 2016 and 2020. Patient L, a 25-year-old man with paraplegia, panic disorder, and ADHD, was continued on Adderall 60 mg daily (above the maximum recommended dose, without documented rationale or vital signs) and started on alprazolam 1 mg, zolpidem 10 mg, and paroxetine without documented informed consent or a CURES check. One week later the psychiatrist tripled alprazolam to 3 mg daily with an early refill and no office visit, then raised it to 3.5 mg and 4 mg daily even after the patient admitted taking more than prescribed, without addressing possible misuse or diversion.

Patient B, a 24-year-old woman with schizophrenia and ADHD, reported command auditory hallucinations to harm herself in 2018 and again in 2020; according to the Accusation, no suicide risk assessment was done, antipsychotics were left at low doses despite persistent psychosis, and stimulants were continued and even increased after she admitted overusing methylphenidate. Benzodiazepine and stimulant changes were made without visits, prescriptions issued in 2019 were not documented, and CURES was not checked until months into treatment, with no note that she was receiving oxycodone and hydrocodone elsewhere. Patient S, a 42-year-old man with persistent depression and ADHD, was given lorazepam and later alprazolam while receiving opioids and carisoprodol from other prescribers, with no documented opioid-benzodiazepine risk discussion, no suicide risk assessment despite repeated reports of worsening depression, and lorazepam issued twice after the chart said it had been stopped.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 4 years' probation with controlled-substance log, 30-hour/year education course, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, and practice monitor; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery $4,960.

narrative: The psychiatrist did not contest that the Board could establish a factual basis for the charges in the First Amended Accusation, which alleged the following. Between May 2016 and September 2017, the psychiatrist treated Patient 1 in an outpatient practice, through in-person and telephone sessions and text messages, for depression and anxiety. At intake the psychiatrist diagnosed major depression and prescribed Cymbalta, added Klonopin (clonazepam) as needed for anxiety and sleep, and a few weeks later added an ADHD diagnosis and Adderall based on the patient's report of lifelong difficulty organizing tasks. The Accusation alleged that none of these diagnoses was supported by a documented history, mental status examination, psychiatric or medical history, or substance use history, even though the intake form listed polysubstance abuse and the patient disclosed past and ongoing alcohol and GHB use. Over the following year the psychiatrist learned the patient missed an appointment while intoxicated, was drinking to console herself, and once offered a large jar of marijuana in lieu of payment, yet conducted no substance use assessment, did no monitoring or testing, and documented no discussion of the risks of combining alcohol or GHB with a benzodiazepine.

The psychiatrist wrote monthly prescriptions for 90 tablets each of Klonopin and Adderall, far more than the instructed doses, and in June 2017 issued two prescriptions of each, explaining to investigators that she wanted the patient to have extra medication on hand. The patient's condition deteriorated (a work "meltdown," disability leave, appearing at work intoxicated) without any change in the treatment plan. In August 2017 the patient stopped her medications on her own, developed suicidal thoughts and severe anxiety, and was treated at a detoxification facility for sedative-hypnotic withdrawal and a severe sedative-hypnotic use disorder.
