Patient B, about 55, with anxiety, panic, OCD, and ADHD, received lisdexamfetamine 70 mg, alprazolam 1 mg (#75 per 25 days), bupropion, and aripiprazole while other clinicians prescribed him opioids; the psychiatrist tracked his elevated liver enzymes and advised him to stop drinking. Patient C, 49, with generalized anxiety and panic disorder with agoraphobia and insomnia, received diazepam, alprazolam, lorazepam, and sublingual zolpidem monthly while also filling occasional opioid prescriptions from others.

After a five-day hearing, the administrative law judge, finding the Board's expert biased and the defense expert more persuasive, found that the benzodiazepine prescribing was reasonable and not excessive, that mental status examinations were performed, and that CURES checks were not mandatory before October 2018 (after which he checked CURES for all three). The only violation found was that he did not document informed-consent discussions of the risks and benefits of the controlled substances he prescribed; the judge credited his testimony that those discussions occurred and found this a records violation, not a departure from the standard of care. All other causes were dismissed, and a public reprimand was imposed below the guideline minimum, citing good care, no prior discipline, and improved record keeping.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand, conditioned on completing a Board-approved medical record keeping course within 90 days.

narrative: The psychiatrist worked at an inpatient psychiatric hospital. According to the Accusation, in May 2017 he assumed care of Patient A, a minor girl with recurrent major depressive disorder admitted on an involuntary hold after statements of self-harm. When her father asked for her discharge, the psychiatrist, believing she was not ready, placed a second 72-hour hold, and a certification review hearing upheld continued involuntary treatment. The Accusation alleged that the physician's orders and legal-holds sections of the chart were inconsistent and at times did not accurately show whether she was voluntary or involuntary, and that although the chart showed her parents were separated and her mother lived out of state, there was no documentation of custody or of the mother's consent, and he failed to identify and document who could consent to treatment for the minor.

In 2019 he treated Patient B, admitted on a grave-disability hold in a manic, disorganized state with hypertension, abnormal liver and renal tests, and an alcohol detoxification protocol, who twice needed transfer to the emergency department. She was diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, and repeatedly refused antipsychotics; the psychiatrist obtained two court orders permitting involuntary medication (including quetiapine, haloperidol, risperidone, chlorpromazine, ziprasidone, and lithium). The Accusation alleged his physician's orders did not reflect her changing legal status or the first court order authorizing involuntary medication, there were no physician's orders at all for several days, and he failed to diagnose or document alcohol withdrawal, including in the discharge summary when she left against medical advice. It charged gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, inadequate records, and unprofessional conduct, including intentional violation of involuntary inpatients' rights. He did not admit the allegations but agreed a prima facie case could be established; the public reprimand states that he failed to consistently and accurately document pertinent medical and legal information for both patients.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand (issued upon completion of coursework) with 40 hours of education, medical record keeping course, and professionalism program (ethics course); must cease practice if courses are not completed on time.

narrative: The psychiatrist agreed that the Board could establish a prima facie case for the charges in the First Amended Accusation, which alleged repeated negligent acts and inadequate records in the outpatient medication management of three patients between 2015 and 2021. According to the Accusation, nearly every visit note lacked a narrative interval history and clinical assessment; the subjective entries were brief "provider notes" or chief complaints that the psychiatrist said nursing staff recorded, and after an electronic record change the treatment plan routinely read "continue current medications" even at visits where medications were changed. CURES review was never documented, and prescriptions the patients received from other physicians were not recorded.

The Accusation described benzodiazepine prescribing alongside opioids from other prescribers without documented risk discussion. Patient A, treated for depression and anxiety, was switched to alprazolam 0.5 mg twice daily with no follow-up for two months, then increased to 1 mg three times daily without a documented risk assessment, while CURES showed she had been filling monthly hydrocodone and tramadol from other prescribers since January 2016; this was first noted in 2019, when her pain physician asked why she was on Xanax, and alprazolam was stopped without a documented taper plan. Patient B, with bipolar depression and insomnia, received temazepam 15 mg (up to 60 per month) for years while filling hydrocodone elsewhere, with no documented discussion of opioid or alcohol interactions and no reconsideration after a fall requiring emergency back surgery. Patient C's alprazolam was raised to 1 mg twice daily while she was taking morphine and later OxyContin and oxycodone, with no documented discussion of combining a benzodiazepine with two opioids.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand (relating to medical record keeping) with 40-hour education course, medical record keeping course, and prescribing practices course; cost recovery $5,708.75.

cases.type: Public reprimand / public letter of reprimand
narrative: According to the Board's Public Letter of Reprimand, an investigation by the Medical Board of California revealed that the psychiatrist deviated from the standard of care by failing to adequately document complete mental status examinations and by providing courtesy refills for an inappropriate time or frequency. The letter gives no further facts about the patients, setting, or medications involved.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand issued under the Board's authority to resolve a matter with a public reprimand; no probation terms stated.

narrative: The psychiatrist, practicing for about 45 years with no prior discipline, treated mostly Medi-Cal and Medicare outpatients in a psychiatric medical group. The case began with a complaint from a patient's husband that he kept prescribing Xanax after being warned she was abusing it. After a four-day hearing on charges involving four patients, an administrative law judge found that gross negligence was not proven. The judge did find inadequate records and, on that basis, repeated negligent acts. The judge found that he responded to the husband's call by stopping Xanax when Patient 1, a 30-year-old woman with depression and anxiety, had already tapered herself off. He restarted it six months later after she reported abstinence from alcohol, and he had been pasting CURES reports into the chart. The judge did not find that he failed to assess substance use, and found that contacting the husband without consent would have raised confidentiality concerns. He did not, however, document any discussion of alcohol with Xanax.

The judge found documentation failures for every patient. His notes were copied from prior visits and repeated the same boilerplate treatment plan and goals at every visit for four very different patients over years. Medication changes had no recorded rationale. For Patient 2, an 86-year-old man with dementia, he gave no documented rationale, monitoring, or alternatives for long-term concurrent Restoril and Ativan. For Patient 3, an obese 32-year-old with ADHD and anxiety, he raised Adderall from 80 to 120 mg/day after a phone call he never documented, while the chart said concentration had improved. He also continued Xanax 3 mg/day for years without documenting a rationale or a discussion of SSRI/SNRI alternatives. For Patient 4, he documented no rationale for Latuda and Seroquel and no counseling about combining Xanax and Ambien while she also filled Norco from another prescriber.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand (public reproval) with a Board-approved medical record keeping course within 60 days and cost recovery of $13,302 (reduced 50% from the $26,604.25 requested).

narrative: The psychiatrist, licensed since 1971 and in outpatient practice, admitted only that the Board could establish a prima facie case and accepted a public reprimand stating that between 2009 and 2020 he prescribed controlled substances to three patients while keeping sparse and incomplete records. According to the Accusation, his handwritten notes for all three women were short, hard to read, and rarely recorded examination findings, assessment, interventions, or goals. Patient A, 33 at intake in 2009, was treated for bipolar disorder, attention deficit disorder, and insomnia; from mid-2017 to early 2020 he provided monthly prescriptions for zolpidem, Vyvanse, and amphetamines while documenting only about five or six visits, including a gap of nearly 17 months between visits, which the Accusation alleged was gross negligence.

Patient B, 20 at intake in 2013 with ADHD, anxiety, and panic disorder, reported taking Xanax a few times a week; he added clonazepam in late 2017 and prescribed both benzodiazepines from 2018 to 2019 with no documented reason for either the new prescription or the combination. Patient C, 44 at intake in 2012 with depression, suicidal thoughts, an eating-disorder history, migraine, and later bipolar disorder and ADD, was on multiple medications including lurasidone, lamotrigine, methylphenidate, clonazepam, eszopiclone, and zolpidem. Although he knew she was also seeing a psychologist, neurologist, and pain physician and she had signed a release, the chart held no records from them and no documented coordination. In 2020 he wrote four prescriptions for 15 Percocet tablets each with no documented reason. The Accusation also cited 1989 Board discipline (60-day suspension and probation, terminated in 1996).
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; prescribing practices course and medical record keeping course; costs of $15,426.

narrative: The Accusation concerned two older women whom the psychiatrist treated, largely for general medical problems, while prescribing controlled substances. Patient 1, a 90-year-old woman seen in 2018-2019 for COPD, bronchitis, osteoarthritis, hypothyroidism, and epigastric pain, was prescribed promethazine with codeine from September to December 2018 at the same time as lorazepam and temazepam, plus pregabalin. Patient 2, a 71-year-old woman seen from 2017 to 2020, was already on clonazepam when the psychiatrist began prescribing it in February 2017. She later developed breast cancer and worsening anxiety and depression. The psychiatrist kept her on escitalopram and raised clonazepam from 1 mg three times daily to 1 mg four times daily in mid-2019 and again in 2020. The Accusation alleged that the standard of care for long-term benzodiazepines calls for routine urine toxicology to confirm adherence and rule out diversion, along with monitoring of clinical response and CURES. The psychiatrist said she had reviewed CURES but did not document it, and she ordered no urine toxicology screens.

For both patients, every electronic record entry listed a different physician as the provider because of an apparent system defect, and the psychiatrist added signed handwritten notes. Several entries showed "error message" in place of medication reconciliation, and others carried forward medication lists that had not been updated. The Accusation charged repeated negligent acts and inadequate records and cited prior discipline from 2011: a stayed revocation with seven years' probation for gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, prescribing without examination, inadequate records, and excessive prescribing. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established; she made no admissions. The reprimand states that from 2017 to 2020 she kept incomplete and unclear records for two patients to whom she prescribed controlled substances.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand with prescribing practices course and medical record keeping course; cost recovery $18,000.

narrative: The Accusation concerned two outpatients to whom the psychiatrist prescribed benzodiazepines. It stated that the prescribing itself was appropriate and faulted only the documentation of informed consent. Patient 1 was treated for anxiety from July 2019 to November 2020. The psychiatrist continued clonazepam that another provider had started and, in October 2020, added temazepam 30 mg at bedtime. Patient 2, first seen in November 2018 and diagnosed with bipolar disorder and depression, was started on alprazolam 0.5 mg three times daily as needed for panic attacks in April 2020. For both patients, the Accusation alleged that he did not document an informed consent discussion covering the risks, benefits, and alternatives before prescribing these controlled substances, and it charged this as repeated negligent acts and inadequate records. It also cited a 2018 Public Letter of Reprimand for failing to obtain baseline laboratory tests for a patient, failing to justify in writing a maintenance medication dose above the manufacturer's recommended dose, and omitting important documentation.

In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist did not contest that the complainant could establish a prima facie case or factual basis for the charges and gave up his right to contest them; he made no admissions. The reprimand states that in 2020 he failed to document informed consent when prescribing benzodiazepines to two patients.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand with medical record keeping course; cost recovery $8,000.

cases.type: Public reprimand / public letter of reprimand
narrative: According to the Public Letter of Reprimand, a Board investigation found that between 2019 and 2023, for three patients, the psychiatrist made insufficient entries in the psychiatric records and finalized chart entries late, did not document the required CURES database checks, and failed to document medication informed-consent discussions and medication monitoring. The Board characterized this as repeated negligent acts and failure to maintain adequate records.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand with conditions: complete a medical record keeping course and reimburse costs of $11,382.

narrative: The psychiatrist owned an outpatient clinic, later converted to a federally qualified health center where he worked as an independent contractor. He also worked long shifts, often 12 or 24 hours, as a psychiatrist at a state prison. According to the Accusation, from 2017 to 2019 a physician assistant trained in family and internal medicine provided much of the monthly medication-management care for three clinic patients. Each had major depressive disorder with psychotic features and PTSD and was treated with antipsychotics (quetiapine, aripiprazole), antidepressants, and in one case zolpidem. For dozens of visits, the charts were electronically signed by the psychiatrist on days when his prison time records showed he was on shift and could not have been at the clinic, which he confirmed. Pharmacy records showed the physician assistant had sent the refill prescriptions, but the assistant's signature appeared nowhere in the charts. Some refills were duplicated days apart or sent on dates with no chart entry.

The Accusation described the notes as largely cloned from visit to visit, with unexplained short-interval return visits and contradictory data, such as one patient's height recorded as 67, 61, and 64 inches and a 15-pound weight swing with no comment. When asked, the psychiatrist could not produce a delegation of services agreement or drug formulary for 2017-2019 and signed a new one only in 2022. He said he did not know why the assistant had not signed the charts and thought he was co-signing them. The assistant's psychiatric training consisted of shadowing him for about two weeks, with no documented education or competency assessment. The Accusation charged repeated negligent acts, inadequate records, and failure to have a delegation of services agreement. In the stipulated settlement he did not contest that a prima facie case could be established and gave up his right to contest the charges; he made no admissions.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with 40 hours/year of education, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism program (ethics course), practice and billing monitor, solo practice prohibition, notification of hospitals/facilities/insurers, and prohibition on supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery $31,075.75.

narrative: The psychiatrist, whose only training was in psychiatry and who worked full-time elsewhere as an employed psychiatrist, admitted the truth of every charge and allegation in the Accusation, which charged unprofessional conduct and gross negligence arising from a medical aesthetics clinic he co-owned and nominally directed.

According to the admitted allegations, the psychiatrist and his then-wife, a registered nurse, jointly owned a cosmetic clinic offering Botox and dermal filler injections, thread lifts, laser hair removal, and skin tag removal, and he served as its chief executive officer and medical director while working off-site. The nurse was the only person who treated patients; the psychiatrist never saw, examined, or consulted on any patient there, had no training or knowledge of the procedures, established no policies or procedures, and acknowledged that she practiced unsupervised. From 2018 to 2021 she treated patients without supervision, and from August 2018 to May 2019 on an expired nursing license. The matter came to the Board through a 2019 complaint from a patient who alleged that the nurse injected Botox into her and a friend with the same needle, that a thread lift left scarring, and that the products used were not what was claimed; the clinic said it had misplaced her records. In the records of six other patients, the psychiatrist's stamped signature appeared on consultation notes for patients he had never met, some of whom were former hospital co-workers. In a 2023 Board interview he could not describe a medical director's duties, said he had told the nurse to hire another physician for examinations but did not know whether she had, and called it his error for trusting her.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 4 years' probation with 40 hours/year of education, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program; no solo practice; prohibited from performing dermal fillers, Botox, Juvederm, threading, and laser hair and skin tag removal, and from serving as an off-site medical director, with patient notification; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; costs of $40,919.25.

narrative: The psychiatrist had been placed on five years' probation effective May 2015 under a stipulated settlement in which he admitted the allegations of a 2014 Accusation: after his license had lapsed into delinquent status, he faxed a state hospital's medical staff office a pocket license whose expiration date had been altered to appear current, and he signed a medical staff application listing that false expiration date and attesting that his license had never been not renewed; he renewed the license only after the hospital learned from the Board that it was delinquent.

The Petition to Revoke Probation alleged that he failed to pay the annual probation monitoring costs required by his probation. At the hearing, which proceeded by default because he did not appear, the administrative law judge found that he had been told in 2015 that costs (then $4,106 per year) were due each January 31, that a $400-per-month payment plan was arranged in late 2016 after he had made no payments, and that he made a $400 payment in March 2017 but did not keep up payments. He did not pay $15,473 by a February 2020 deadline, and by May 2020 he owed $21,904; he acknowledged to his probation inspector that he was behind and understood that nonpayment could lead to further discipline. The judge noted he was otherwise compliant apart from some late quarterly reports. Finding a violation of the cost-payment condition and no mitigating evidence, the judge set aside the stay and imposed the revocation.
cases.outcome: Probation revoked; stayed revocation imposed and license revoked.

narrative: The psychiatrist was already on three years' probation under a 2019 stipulated settlement resolving an Accusation for dangerous use of alcohol and a criminal conviction. According to that Accusation, in 2016 police followed a trail of radiator fluid from a telephone pole that had been struck by a car to the psychiatrist's home, where they found him lying on the ground near his damaged car; he admitted drinking several alcoholic beverages before driving, showed signs of intoxication, and preliminary breath tests showed a blood alcohol content of roughly 0.26% to 0.29%. He pleaded no contest to driving with a blood alcohol content of 0.08% or more and admitted a special allegation that it was 0.15% or greater. Probation terms included complete abstinence from alcohol and controlled substances, biological fluid testing, a professionalism (ethics) program, psychiatric evaluation, and psychotherapy.

The Petition to Revoke Probation alleged that he violated the condition requiring complete abstinence from alcohol: a biological fluid sample collected in July 2021 tested positive for phosphatidylethanol, consistent with ingestion of alcohol, and he admitted having consumed an alcoholic beverage within a week before the sample. A Cease Practice Order was issued in August 2021. In the stipulated surrender, the psychiatrist did not admit the allegations but agreed that the complainant could establish a factual basis for the charges and gave up his right to contest them.
cases.outcome: License surrendered; if he ever petitions for reinstatement, the Petition to Revoke Probation allegations will be deemed true and admitted.

narrative: The psychiatrist, a child and adult psychiatrist, had her license revoked in 2005 for cocaine use and impairment after relapses in the Board's diversion program and residential treatment. The license was reinstated on five years' probation in January 2019, with complete abstinence from alcohol and random biological fluid testing. After a three-day hearing on a First Amended Petition to Revoke Probation, an administrative law judge found that she committed major probation violations. She drank champagne at a wedding in June 2019, failed to test when selected while traveling in June 2021 (the site she went to was closed), and had positive alcohol tests in July 2021 (blood PEth 45.1) and October/November 2021. The July 2021 result followed drinking beer and possibly vodka during a period of grief over her brother's death. The October 2021 result was attributed to rum in a birthday pie. As aggravation, the judge found the 2005 revocation, a missed test in June 2019, and ten positive tests between January and September 2019, many at very low levels and attributed to rum cake, liqueur in coffee, food, and a vaginal wipe. Those 2019 results had already led to a cease-practice order and two citations with fines.

The judge found no evidence of cocaine use since 2014. A Board-ordered clinical diagnostic evaluation found cocaine use disorder in remission, major depressive disorder, no alcohol use disorder, and that she could practice safely. It also found that her alcohol use showed poor insight and judgment. The judge found that she had 22 months of negative tests, completed an outpatient program, added Soberlink monitoring, and had been in psychotherapy and TMS for depression. Revocation was rejected, but probation was restarted for a full five years, with an ethics course and psychotherapy added.
cases.outcome: Probation revoked and stayed revocation imposed, then stayed again; new five-year probation with abstinence from controlled substances and alcohol, biological fluid testing, 10 hours of community service, professionalism (ethics) program, psychotherapy, medical evaluation and treatment, and prohibition on supervising PAs and advanced practice nurses.

narrative: This short Agreement for Surrender of License concerns a psychiatrist who was already on Board probation. According to the agreement, an Accusation had been filed against him in February 2021, and an August 2021 decision revoked his license, stayed the revocation, and placed him on three years' probation with standard terms and conditions. That probation order allowed him to request voluntary surrender if he stopped practicing because of retirement or health reasons or was otherwise unable to satisfy the terms and conditions of probation. Invoking that condition, he agreed to surrender his license, wallet and wall certificates, and any California DEA registration, and the Board accepted the surrender in February 2023. The agreement does not describe the conduct underlying the 2021 Accusation, does not state which probation terms he could not meet, and does not allege any probation violation; at the time, his address of record was outside California.

Earlier decision (summarized in this document as CA-160-58): the 2021 probation was reciprocal discipline. After a hearing, an administrative law judge found that another state's medical commission had disciplined him for failing, as medical director of outpatient substance use disorder clinics, to prevent his signature from being used to order medically unnecessary urine drug testing billed to insurers, and for prescribing buprenorphine-naloxone and benzodiazepines to a friend and colleague without checking the prescription monitoring program while the friend was receiving opioids from six other providers.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; any future application for relicensure or reinstatement to be treated as a petition for reinstatement of a revoked license, with Board investigation reports admissible and time-based defenses waived.

narrative: The psychiatrist, a geriatric psychiatrist licensed in 2000, had been on Board probation for over ten years. In 2012 she admitted gross and repeated negligence while employed by a large medical group, including failing to properly manage patients' medications, assess a patient's psychosis in relation to her medical status, take adequate histories, and manage patients with substance abuse; she was placed on four years' probation with a billing monitor and courses. In 2016, after an Accusation alleging that in private practice she pressured patients to pay for multiple assessment sessions, failed to keep records of an examination, and had no written billing or payment policies, her probation was extended by 35 months with conditions including a billing monitor and a cap of two years of non-practice, with a clinical training program required after 18 months of non-practice.

After a hearing, an administrative law judge found that she went about six months without a billing monitor before enrolling in a professional enhancement program, which suspended her in August 2019 because she had submitted no patient lists since March 2019 and no chart notes or billing information for that year. The Board issued a cease-practice order in November 2019, and she did not practice for two years. When she then enrolled in a clinical competence program, it required a psychiatric fitness-for-duty evaluation, and the evaluators reported she was not fit for duty, so she did not complete the program. The judge found violations of the billing-monitor and non-practice/clinical-training conditions. A separate Accusation alleging she was unsafe to practice because of mental illness was dismissed because the evaluators did not testify and their report was hearsay; her own evaluator found her fit. The judge noted that she denied the original misconduct, blamed her probation monitors, and gave no assurance of future compliance.
cases.outcome: Petition to revoke probation granted; license revoked. Accompanying Accusation (mental-illness impairment under B&P 822) dismissed.

narrative: This is a short agreement for surrender of license made while the psychiatrist was on Board probation. An Accusation had been filed in June 2022, and a Decision in October 2023 revoked the license, stayed the revocation, and placed the psychiatrist on 35 months' probation with standard terms. That probation order allowed a request to surrender if the psychiatrist stopped practicing for retirement or health reasons or was otherwise unable to meet the probation terms. Shortly after the order, the psychiatrist used this provision to surrender the license, and the Board's Executive Director accepted it.

The agreement does not describe the conduct alleged in the underlying Accusation, does not say why the psychiatrist could not meet the probation terms, and does not allege any probation violation. No findings or admissions about patient care appear in this document.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; may no longer practice in California; must surrender wallet and wall certificates and any California DEA certificates; any future application treated as a petition for reinstatement of a revoked license.

narrative: This is a short agreement for surrender of license made while the psychiatrist was on Board probation. An Accusation had been filed in September 2022, and a Decision in August 2023 revoked the license, stayed the revocation, and placed the psychiatrist on three years' probation with standard terms. That probation order allowed a request to surrender if the psychiatrist stopped practicing for retirement or health reasons or was otherwise unable to meet the probation terms. A few months into probation, the psychiatrist used this provision to surrender the license, and the Board's Executive Director accepted it.

The agreement does not describe the conduct alleged in the underlying Accusation, does not say why the psychiatrist could not meet the probation terms, and does not allege any probation violation. No findings or admissions about patient care appear in this document.

Earlier decision (summarized in this document as CA-167-28): the 2023 probation resolved an Accusation alleging years of benzodiazepine and other controlled-substance prescribing to three women despite ongoing drinking, overdoses, early refills, and opioids from other prescribers, with almost no CURES checks or drug screens, no suicide risk assessment despite documented self-harm, and poorly legible records. He did not contest that a prima facie case could be established.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; may no longer practice in California; must surrender wallet and wall certificates and any California DEA certificates; any future application treated as a petition for reinstatement of a revoked license.

narrative: This is a short agreement for surrender of license made while the psychiatrist was on Board probation. An Accusation had been filed in December 2020, and a Decision in December 2021 revoked the license, stayed the revocation, and placed the psychiatrist on five years' probation with standard terms. That probation order allowed a request to surrender if the psychiatrist stopped practicing for retirement or health reasons or was otherwise unable to meet the probation terms. About two years and three months into probation, the psychiatrist used this provision to surrender the license, and the Board's Executive Director accepted it.

The agreement does not describe the conduct alleged in the underlying Accusation, does not say why the psychiatrist could not meet the probation terms, and does not allege any probation violation. No findings or admissions about patient care appear in this document.

Earlier decision (summarized in this document as CA-161-2): the 2021 probation resolved an Accusation alleging that a mental illness impaired the psychiatrist's ability to practice safely. According to that Accusation, a Board-approved evaluator reported that she had admitted to an inappropriate relationship with a patient and did not understand doctor-patient boundaries; the probation barred her from practicing until she completed a professional boundaries program and was found mentally fit. She did not admit the allegations, agreeing only that a prima facie case could be established.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; may no longer practice in California; must surrender wallet and wall certificates and any California DEA certificates; any future application treated as a petition for reinstatement of a revoked license.

narrative: This is a short Agreement for Surrender of License signed while the psychiatrist was on probation. It recites that a Second Amended Accusation had been filed against her in March 2020 and that an October 2020 Decision revoked her license, stayed the revocation, and placed her on 35 months' probation with standard terms. That probation order allowed her to request surrender if she stopped practicing for retirement or health reasons or was otherwise unable to satisfy the probation terms, and she used that provision to surrender. The document does not describe the conduct behind the original Accusation or any specific probation violation, and it contains no findings or admissions about the underlying allegations. By its terms, any future application for licensure would be treated as a petition for reinstatement of a revoked license.

Earlier decision (October 2020; it predates the newsletter volumes covered here and was retrieved separately from the Board's Winter 2021 newsletter): the probation resolved a Second Amended Accusation prompted by a complaint that she might be excessively prescribing controlled substances to a family member. It alleged that she prescribed stimulants (Adderall, dextroamphetamine, and Vyvanse) to three patients diagnosed with ADD without any comprehensive evaluation supporting the diagnosis, including supratherapeutic Adderall doses combined with Vyvanse without documented justification, and that she kept inadequate records. It also cited a 2015 Texas Medical Board agreed order, in which she admitted prescribing controlled substances and other medications to a person with whom she had a close personal relationship without a documented immediate need, resulting in a public reprimand in Texas. In the California settlement she admitted the Texas discipline and denied the other charges.
cases.outcome: Surrender of license accepted by the Executive Director on behalf of the Board (under a probation term allowing surrender when unable to satisfy probation); any future application to be treated as a petition for reinstatement; no cost recovery stated.

narrative: The psychiatrist had been placed on four years' probation by a 2023 stipulated settlement of an Accusation alleging gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, and inadequate records. That earlier Accusation, attached to this decision, alleged that he closed his outpatient private practice of roughly 50-60 patients in 2020 by mailing (uncertified) termination letters that gave no referrals or resources, no instructions for obtaining records, and no crisis guidance, without facilitating transfer of care. It also alleged that on an inpatient unit he started a 23-year-old woman with psychosis on Clozaril at 50 mg daily and tripled the dose to 150 mg after two days (the labeling recommends starting at 12.5-25 mg with 25-50 mg increments), repeatedly failed to document which medications and doses she was receiving, and that she later had a new-onset seizure.

The Accusation and Petition to Revoke Probation in this case alleged that the psychiatrist failed the clinical competence assessment program required by his probation: in September 2024 his performance was rated "Fail - Category 4," not meeting the minimum standards for safe patient care, with inadequate knowledge of care and treatment recommendations for several common psychiatric concerns, including omissions that could have harmed patients. The Board issued a cease-practice order. In the stipulated settlement he gave up the right to contest that a prima facie case could be established; there were no findings or admissions.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; three years' probation, concurrent with existing probation (whose terms remain in effect); must complete a clinical competence assessment program before resuming practice (cease-practice order remains until then), practice monitor (or professional enhancement program), prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery of $6,500.00.

narrative: The psychiatrist was already on probation: after an Accusation filed in August 2022, a May 2024 Board decision revoked her license, stayed the revocation, and placed her on three years' probation with standard terms and conditions. This document does not describe the conduct underlying that earlier discipline. Relying on the probation condition that allows a licensee who stops practicing for retirement or health reasons, or who is otherwise unable to satisfy the terms and conditions of probation, to request surrender, the psychiatrist signed an agreement to surrender her license, which the Board accepted. No new misconduct or probation violation is alleged in the document, and nothing was found or admitted.

Earlier decision (summarized in this document as CA-169-97): the 2024 probation resolved an Accusation alleging that, over about three years, she prescribed medications including modafinil, zolpidem, lorazepam, and tramadol to three adult relatives without appropriate examinations or medical records; the probation prohibited her from treating family members. She did not contest that a prima facie case could be established.
cases.outcome: License surrendered; any future application will be treated as a petition for reinstatement of a revoked license.

narrative: The psychiatrist had been placed on 35 months' probation by a Board decision effective November 20, 2025, resolving an Accusation filed in 2023 (summarized separately as CA-173-65, concerning delayed prescribing and late documentation for jail patients). Under the standard probation condition allowing a probationer who stops practicing for retirement or health reasons, or who is otherwise unable to satisfy the terms and conditions of probation, to request surrender, she signed an Agreement for Surrender of License, which the Board's Executive Director accepted. The agreement does not allege any new misconduct or any specific probation violation, and it does not state why she was unable to comply with the terms.
cases.outcome: Surrender of license accepted under the probation surrender condition; wallet certificate, wall license, and any California DEA registration surrendered; any reapplication treated as a petition for reinstatement of a revoked license, with investigation reports admissible and time-based defenses waived.

narrative: The physician, licensed in another state since 1984 with experience in laboratory medicine and addiction medicine, held a California license only to serve as medical director of a laboratory serving California clients. From 2014 to 2017 he was paid medical director of several outpatient substance use disorder clinics in the other state. That state's medical commission, in a stipulated agreed order in August 2020, found that an owner of some of those clinics ran a scheme requiring patients in intensive outpatient treatment to undergo twice-weekly urine drug tests sent for definitive testing of many substances regardless of medical need, billed to insurers as ordered by the physician; that he either knew or should have known his signature was being used to authorize the unnecessary testing, and was otherwise deficient in his duty as medical director to set and oversee laboratory testing policy. It also found that from 2015 to 2019 he treated a friend and colleague (the owner of a behavioral health agency where he had been medical director) for back pain with buprenorphine-naloxone, later adding zolpidem, alprazolam, and lorazepam, without checking the prescription monitoring program or documenting a detailed history, and kept prescribing while the patient received oxycodone and hydrocodone from six other providers; the commission called this a boundary violation and below the standard of care, while noting it did not cause the patient's 2019 death.

The Board sought reciprocal discipline. After a hearing, an administrative law judge found the out-of-state discipline was for conduct that is also unprofessional in California (facilitating insurance fraud and unsafe prescribing). The physician acknowledged he should have prevented the fraud and let a personal relationship affect his judgment; the judge credited his testimony that he did not knowingly participate in or profit from the fraud and acted to stop it when he learned of it, and noted his completion of a competence assessment and the out-of-state courses. Probation mirroring the other state's order was imposed rather than revocation.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with partial controlled-substance restriction (limited to Schedules III-V and naloxone; no marijuana recommendations), controlled-substance record log, 40 hours/year education, prescribing practices course, professionalism/ethics program, practice and billing monitor, and prohibition on supervising PAs/APNs.

narrative: The California case was based entirely on discipline imposed by the Illinois medical licensing agency, where the psychiatrist practiced. According to the Accusation and the attached Illinois Consent Order (August 2021), the Illinois agency received information that the psychiatrist had prescribed controlled substances without renewing her Illinois controlled substance license, and, while that matter was pending, that she failed to appropriately evaluate and treat a patient in her practice who was experiencing an acute psychiatric episode. The Illinois order does not describe the patient or the episode further. In Illinois the psychiatrist neither admitted nor denied the allegations; she was placed on indefinite probation for a minimum of one year with a practice monitor reviewing ten charts per quarter, 10 hours of CME in psychiatric emergencies and 10 hours in professional responsibility, and a $5,000 fine.
California charged discipline by another state. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established; there were no findings or admissions.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; professionalism program (ethics course) within one year; cost recovery of $10,636.31.
